newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe bids farewell to crowds in French rally.
newsitem.headline: Juppe bids farewell to crowds in French rally.

text.p: The leaders of France's ruling centre-right held their final major campaign rally in Paris on Thursday, appealing to voters to mobilise in Sunday's tight election runoff to head off an upset Socialist victory.

Past disputes and quarrels were momentarily buried as the leaders of the often fractious coalition sat side by side and took the stand in turn, raising storms of boos from their 3,000 supporters at every mention of the left.
For outgoing Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe, the rally was a sad farewell to crowds after two years in power, and the crowd tried to make it easy for him.

The unpopular premier, forced to bow out after the left's first-round upset last Sunday, won a standing ovation after describing the country he had dreamt of building, and the country he did not want.
"I do not want the France of the year 2000 to be even more Socialist than the one we inherited in 1993," he said.
"I want a modern France, trusting initiative, the enterprising spirit and innovation to create wealth and jobs."
Embraced by young Gaullist militants, acclaimed by supporters, the man often decried as a dry technocrat turned emotional.
"This warms my heart as it never has been before," he said. before the conservative leadership broke into the Marseillaise national anthem.
But as they left, right-wing militants repeated their grudges against the man blamed by many as responsible for the right's poor performance.
"He should have left earlier," said a student wearing a Gaullist t-shirt.
The Socialists, routed four years ago, made a stunning recovery by outpolling the right last Sunday and Juppe said in a radio interview earlier in the day they could win in the runoff.
There was no admitting doubts to the crowd. "I trust the French people's common sense. I am confident in our victory," Juppe said.
But a straw poll of militants showed the mood to be more worried than enthusiastic. "It will be tough," several said.

Taking the stand before Juppe were his former foes, reconciled for the sake of unity: fellow-Gaullist ex-premier Edouard Balladur, who unsuccessfully ran against Jacques Chirac in the 1995 presidential election, ex-interior minister Charles Pasqua and ex-defence minister Francois Leotard, who had backed Balladur.
Half of the ticket tipped to take over if the right wins was there: liberal ex-finance minister Alain Madelin, who Juppe sacked in 1995.
The other half, socially-minded Philippe Seguin, who is tipped as prime minister, delivered a speech broadcast live on a giant screen from his Epinal constituency in eastern France.

"The French people want a road map" to find their way through the storm of modern changes, Seguin said."If we fail to give it to them, their wrath will engulf us all, the majority and the opposition," he said.
Despite the joined hands on the stand, criticism welled just below the surface.

"France cannot have a Harlequin's suit, liberal in the morning and Socialist in the evening," Leotard said in an attack which appeared aimed both at the Socialists and the unlikely Seguin-Madelin couple.
The official host of the Paris rally, the capital's Gaullist mayor Jean Tiberi, made only a fleeting appearance.
A black sheep since he and his wife became the target of official corruption probes, Tiberi has been kept at arm's length by other rightist candidates throughout the campaign.
